sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Sigurðr** (*sigurd*) ​— Victory, ‌Dragon-Slaying, Heroism ‌· Victory-guardian (from ​sigr, victory, ​+ vǫrðr, ​guardian) — belongs ​to the ​Norse tradition, ‌where it is ​catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Victory, Dragon-Slaying, Heroism". ​The name ‌means "Victory-guardian ​(from sigr, victory, ‌+ vǫrðr, ​guardian)"[^1].

In ​the norse tradition, ​**Sigurðr** governed ​victory, dragon-slaying, ​heroism. The name ‌encodes a ​sphere of ‌power that shaped ​ritual, narrative, ‌and social ​order.

His is ‌the northern ​form of ‌the greatest heroic ​story the ​Germanic world ‌ever told: the ‌foster-son of ‌a smith ​who reforged his ​father's shattered ‌sword, the ​slayer of the ​dragon Fáfnir, ‌the wooer ​of the valkyrie ​behind the ‌flame, and ​the oath-brother ‌destroyed by the ​very loyalty ​that made ​him great. What ​the Iliad ‌is to ‌Greece, the Vǫlsunga ​cycle is ‌to the ​North.[^2]

PuniCodex restores ​the name ‌as **Sigurðr** ‌and serves its ‌temple at ‌[sigurðr.com](https://xn--sigurr-twa.com). The ​restoration preserves at ‌least one ​distinctive feature ​— a diacritic ​or a ‌distinctive letter ​— that the ​ASCII form ​loses, and ‌exactly one historically ​valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which places the ‌name in ​Tier 1. ‌The plain ASCII ​form *sigurd* ‌survives as ​a modern convenience ‌imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation survives ‌for this ​name; **Sigurðr** ​is a ​scholarly transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed spoken ‌form. Etymologically ​the name ​means "Victory-guardian ‌(from sigr, ​victory, + ‌vǫrðr, guardian)"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII form ​*sigurd* survives ​only because ​the early ​domain-name system ​could not ‌carry diacritics; ​it is ‌a technological ​compromise, not ‌an ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Sigurðr** ‌recovers the ​full diacritic ​detail of ‌the scholarly ‌transliteration directly ‌in the ​address bar. ​The restoration ‌preserves at ​least one ​distinctive feature ‌— a ​diacritic or ​a distinctive ‌letter ​— that ‌the ASCII ​form loses, ​and exactly ​one historically ​valid Unicode ‌restoration exists, ‌which places ​the name ‌in Tier ​1.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ‌**s** → ‌**S** ‌— Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**i** → ​**i** — ​Same
- ​**g** → ‌**g** — ​Same
- ​**u** → ​**u** — ‌Same
- ​**r** → ​**r** — ​Same
‌- **d** ​→ **ðr** ‌— Eth ​ð (voiced ‌dental fricative) ​+ nominative ‌-r of ‌Sigurðr

The ​project holds ​the domain ​**sigurðr.com** (xn--sigurr-twa.com) ​as the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈsiɣ.urðr̩/** ‌— Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by phoneme:

​- **S** — ​Voiceless alveolar sibilant ​[s], as in ​English 'sea'
- ‌**i** — Short close ​front [i]; the ​first syllable carries ‌the stress
- ​**g** — Medial ‌voiced velar fricative ​[ɣ]; between vowels ‌Old Norse g softened ​to a glide, ​closer to the ​Spanish g of ​'lago' than a ​hard stop
- ‌**-urðr** — Short [u], ​alveolar trill [r], ‌the voiced dental ​fricative [ð] — ‌the soft 'th' ​of 'father' — ‌and the final nominative ​ending -r, syllabic ‌after the eth

​For the modern ​speaker, the closest ‌approximation is: 'SIG-urthr' ‌— stress the ‌first syllable, soften the ​middle g almost ​to a glide, ‌sound the ð ​as the soft ​'th' of 'father', ‌and let the final ​-r hang as ​a light voiced ‌syllable; it is ​the Old Norse ‌nominative ending, not ​a separate vowel.

Kindred ​and historical forms ​of the name:

​- **Old Norse** ‌— Sigurðr, the ‌form of the ​Vǫlsunga cycle and the ‌Eddic lays
- ​**Modern Icelandic** — ​Sigurður, the living ‌form with the ‌epenthetic -u- before ‌the final -r
‌- **German** — Siegfried, ​the continental cognate ‌of the Nibelungenlied ​and Wagner's Ring
​- **Anglicized** — ​Sigurd, the conventional ‌English rendering, dropping the ​eth and the ​nominative -r

Sigurðr ​is Tier 1: ‌the eth ð ​is a distinctive ​letter the ASCII form ​loses, and the ‌final -r preserves ​the Old Norse ‌nominative ending that ​English drops entirely. ‌Cleasby-Vigfusson (s.v. Sigurðr) ​and Zoëga (s.v. Sigurðr) ‌record the form ‌as the name ​of the Vǫlsung ​hero; the name ​compounds sigr, 'victory', ​with -vǫrðr, 'guardian', yielding ‌'victory-guardian', and answers ‌to the continental ​German Siegfried.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The original ​script for ‌this norse ‌name has ​not yet ​been added ​to PUNICODEX. ​The form ​shown is ‌a scholarly transliteration.[^1]

​The form ​**Sigurðr** is ‌therefore a ​scholarly transliteration ‌rather than ​an attested ‌ancient spelling; ​it encodes ​the reconstructed sound ​of the ​name for ​modern use, ‌and no ​mark in ‌it is ​decorative.

The ‌medieval Norse wrote ​*Sigurðr* in ‌the Latin ​alphabet the ‌Icelanders adapted ​for their ​vernacular, and ‌it is ‌in that ‌script — Codex ​Regius, the ​*Vǫlsunga saga* ‌manuscripts — ​that the ​name is ‌preserved. The ​hero's own ​age wrote ‌in the Younger ​Futhark, the ‌sixteen-rune alphabet ​carved on ​the memorial ​stones that ​depict his ‌deeds; reduced ‌to sixteen ​signs, it did ‌not even ​distinguish *ð* ​from *þ* ‌or *d* ‌from *t*, ‌so the ‌full sound ​of the ‌name was never ​recoverable from ​runes alone. ​The restored ‌form *Sigurðr* ​keeps both ​features the ​Latin-script manuscripts ‌attest: the eth ​*ð*, the ​voiced dental ​fricative, and ‌the nominative ​ending *-r*. ‌As a ​registrable domain ‌the Unicode ​form carries the ‌eth that ‌the ASCII ​*sigurd* flattens ​to d ​— the ​punycode encodes ‌exactly what ‌the saga ​scribes wrote.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
In the ​norse tradition, ‌**Sigurðr** governed ‌victory, dragon-slaying, heroism. ​The name ​encodes a sphere ​of power ​that shaped ​ritual, narrative, and ‌social order.

​His is ​the northern form ‌of the ​greatest heroic story ‌the Germanic ​world ever ‌told: the foster-son ​of a ​smith who ​reforged his father's ​shattered sword, ​the slayer of ‌the dragon ​Fáfnir, the ‌wooer of the ​valkyrie behind ‌the flame, ​and the oath-brother ‌destroyed by ​the very loyalty ‌that made ​him great. ​What the Iliad ‌is to ‌Greece, the ‌Vǫlsunga cycle is ​to the ​North.[^1]

### Gramr

‌The sword ​Óðinn thrust ​into the tree ‌Barnstokkr and ​only Sigmundr ​could draw; shattered ‌in his ​last battle, reforged ‌by Reginn ​for the ​son who would ​avenge him.

​### Fáfnir ‌at Gnitaheiðr

The ‌brother turned ​dragon by greed, ‌slain by ​a hero ​lying in a ‌trench; from ‌his heart-blood ‌Sigurðr learned the ‌speech of ​birds.

### The ‌Flame-Wall

Through ​the vafrlogi ​on Hindarfjall rode ​Grani's rider ‌to wake ​Brynhildr, the valkyrie ​Óðinn had ​sunk in sleep ‌— the ​oath sworn ​there could not ​survive the ‌world of ​men.

### The ‌Cursed Hoard

​Andvari's gold, paid ‌as weregild ​for Ótr ‌and cursed at ‌its surrender; ​every hand ​it passed through ​— Hreiðmarr, ​Fáfnir, Sigurðr, the ‌Gjúkings — ‌it brought ​to ruin.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with Sigurðr ‌concentrates ​in a ​small ​set of ​recurring attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement ​about the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**Gramr** ‌— The ​reforged sword ‌of ​Sigmundr, drawn ​from ​Barnstokkr and ​mended by ​Reginn; ‌with it ​Sigurðr ‌slew Fáfnir
​- **Grani** ‌— ​The grey ‌horse ​of Sleipnir's ‌line who ​bore ​Sigurðr through ‌the flame-wall ‌and ‌carried the ​dragon's ​gold from ‌Gnitaheiðr
- ​**Andvaranautr ​and the ‌hoard** ​— The ​dwarf Andvari's ‌ring ​and gold, ‌taken as ​ransom ​and cursed ​at ​the taking ‌— the ‌engine ​of every ‌death ​in the ​cycle
- ‌**The ‌dragon's heart-blood** ‌— Roasting ‌Fáfnir's ​heart, Sigurðr ‌tasted ​the blood ​and understood ​the ‌birds — ​knowledge ​bought from ​the monster ‌he ​killed
- ​**The ​vafrlogi flame-wall** ‌— The ​ring ‌of fire ​around the ‌sleeping ​Brynhildr, crossable ‌only ‌by the ​destined rider; ​crossed ​twice, once ​for ‌love and ‌once in ​betrayal

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
**Sigurðr** is the dragonslayer of ​the Vǫlsunga cycle, the Norse original of the ‌German Siegfried and the last great hero of ‌the legendary North. Son of Sigmundr and Hjǫrdís, ​fostered by the smith Reginn, he reforged his ​father's sword, killed the dragon Fáfnir, and woke ​the valkyrie Brynhildr from her enchanted sleep — ​then lost her, and his life, to a ​draught of forgetfulness and the plotting of his ‌sworn brothers. His story survives in the Poetic ​Edda, the Prose Edda, and Vǫlsunga saga, and ​through the Middle High German Nibelungenlied it became ‌the backbone of Wagner's Ring. Where the gods ​of the Edda face a doom they know ‌is coming, Sigurðr faces one he has forgotten ​— and that is the more human tragedy.[^1]

‌### The Reforging of Gramr (Vǫlsunga saga)

At ​the wedding feast of his sister Signý, a ​one-eyed stranger — Óðinn himself — thrust a ​sword to the hilt into the tree Barnstokkr ​that grew through the hall of Vǫlsungr, and ​only Sigmundr of all the company could draw ‌it. Years later Sigmundr fell in battle, the sword ​shattering beneath him against the same god's spear, ‌and his widow Hjǫrdís carried the shards away ​for her unborn son. That son, Sigurðr, was ‌fostered by Reginn, a smith of the dwarf-kin, ​who urged him against the dragon Fáfnir and ‌forged blade after blade that broke under the ​boy's testing.

Only the shards of his father's ‌sword held. Reginn reforged them into *Gramr*, and ​Sigurðr clove the smith's anvil to the stock ​and sheared a tuft of wool drifting downstream ‌as though it were stone. The episode binds ‌the hero to Óðinn from birth: the god ‌who gave the sword also broke it, and ​the blade that passes from father to son ​is the visible thread of a destiny the ‌boy never chose.[^2]

### The Slaying of Fáfnir ​(Fáfnismál)

Fáfnir was Reginn's brother, who killed their ​father Hreiðmarr for the hoard paid as weregild ‌for the slain Ótr and crawled away to ​Gnitaheiðr, where greed long brooding over gold twisted ​him into a dragon. Guided by a one-eyed ‌old man, Sigurðr dug a trench across the dragon's ​path to the water and lay in it; ‌when Fáfnir crawled overhead, he thrust Gramr upward ​into the heart. The dying dragon questioned his ​slayer and warned him that the gold would ​be his death — a warning Sigurðr answered ​with the hero's creed that every man must ‌die, and wealth must serve until that day.

‌Roasting the dragon's heart for Reginn, Sigurðr burned ​his finger and set it in his mouth, ‌and the heart-blood opened the speech of birds ​to him: the nuthatches in the branches warned ​that Reginn meant to kill him. He cut ‌off the smith's head, loaded the cursed hoard ‌onto Grani, and rode away the richest and ‌most doomed man in the North. The birds ‌that save him here will not be there ​at the end.

### The Ale of Forgetfulness ‌(Guðrúnarkviða)

Sigurðr rode through the vafrlogi, the flame-wall ​on Hindarfjall, and woke Brynhildr, the valkyrie Óðinn ​had pricked with the sleep-thorn; they plighted their ​troth and parted. At the court of Gjúki's ‌sons, the queen Grímhildr brewed him the ale of ​forgetfulness, and Brynhildr passed from his mind as ​if she had never been. He married Guðrún, ​swore oaths with her brothers Gunnarr and Hǫgni, ‌and when Gunnarr sought Brynhildr's hand and could ​not cross the flames, Sigurðr exchanged shapes with ​him and rode the fire in his likeness ​— wooing his own forgotten beloved for another ‌man, with a drawn sword laid between them ​in the bed.

The deception could not hold. ‌Brynhildr learned from a ring and a quarrel ​at the river what had been done, and ‌wounded in her pride she demanded Sigurðr's death. ​The brothers, bound to him by oath, incited ‌the unsworn Guthormr, who stabbed Sigurðr as he ‌slept; some lays — *Sigurðarkviða en skamma* and ​Guðrún's own laments — have him slain instead ​out of doors, in the forest. The texts ​disagree on the place but not on the ​meaning: the hoard's curse had reached the man ‌who thought himself above it, through the only ‌weapon that could touch him, the trust of ​those he called his own.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Sigurðr is ​the northern ‌twin of ‌a pan-Germanic ​hero. The ​continental tradition ​— preserved ​in the Middle ​High German ‌*Nibelungenlied* (c. ​1200), the ​*Lied vom ‌Hürnen Seyfrid*, ​and the ‌Old Norse *Þiðreks ​saga*, which ‌repatriates German ​material — ​tells of ​the same ​dragon-fight, hoard, and ​betrayal under ‌the name ​Siegfried, with ‌the details ​reworked: the ‌valkyrie becomes ​a Burgundian queen, ‌the flame-wall ​drops away, ‌and the ​murder moves ​to a ‌forest spring. ‌Scholars have long ‌read the ​cycle's skeleton ​against history, ‌seeing in ​Gunnarr and ​the fall ‌of the Gjúkings ​the shadow ​of the ‌Burgundian kingdom ​destroyed by ‌the Huns ​in 437 — ​legend crystallized ​around remembered ​catastrophe. The ‌dragon-slaying itself ‌belongs to ​a still ‌older inheritance: the ​Indo-European formula ​of the ‌hero who ‌kills the ‌serpent, traced ‌by Calvert ​Watkins through Indra ‌and Vṛtra, ​Herakles and ​the Lernaean ​hydra, and ‌Beowulf's fatal ​last fight. ​In later folklore ​the story ‌lived on ​in the ​Faroese *Sjúrðar ​kvæði* ballads, ‌still sung and ​danced in ‌the islands ​centuries after ‌the saga ​manuscripts were ‌copied.[^1]

Within ‌the Norse tradition, ​closely related ​names in ​the corpus ​include [[alfheimr|Álfheimr]], ‌[[bifrost|Bifrǫst]], [[buri|Búri]], ‌[[eggther|Eggþér]], [[fafnir|Fáfnir]], ​and [[helheimr|Helheimr]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: No Norse ​figure has ‌had a ‌longer second life. ​William Morris ​retold the ​cycle in his ​epic *The ​Story of ‌Sigurd the Volsung ​and the ​Fall of ‌the Niblungs* ​(1876), which he ‌called the ​great story ‌of the North ​that should ​be to ​all his race ​what the ​tale of ‌Troy was to ​the Greeks. ‌Richard Wagner ​made it the ‌armature of ​*Der Ring ‌des Nibelungen* — ​*Siegfried* and ‌*Götterdämmerung* follow ​the Norse sources ​where the ‌*Nibelungenlied* had ‌softened them, ‌restoring the valkyrie ​Brünnhilde to ​the centre. ‌Arthur Rackham's illustrations ​fixed the ​cycle's visual ‌grammar for a ​century, and ​J. R. ‌R. Tolkien, who ​read the ‌Eddas closely, ​composed his own ​*The Legend ​of Sigurd ​and Gudrún* in ‌Eddic metre. ‌The dragonslayer ​persists in opera ‌houses, novels, ​games, and ​film wherever ‌a hero wins ‌gold and ‌is destroyed ‌by it. In ​modern heathenry ‌Sigurðr is ​honoured less as ​an object ​of cult ‌than as the ​model of ​the heroic ​ethic — courage ‌held fast ​inside a ​fate already written ​— and ‌the runestones ​that depict him ‌are among ​the tradition's ‌most cited ​monuments. Restoring *Sigurðr* ‌in Unicode ‌keeps the ​eth and the ​nominative -r ​that the ​German Siegfried and ‌the anglicized ‌Sigurd alike ​have lost.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The Sigurðr ​cycle is ‌the most ‌widely depicted heroic ​legend of ​the Viking ​Age. The Ramsund ​carving (Sö ​101) in ‌Södermanland, Sweden, shows ​the whole ​Gnitaheiðr episode ‌in one frame ​— Sigurðr ‌piercing the ​serpent from below, ‌the heart ​roasting over ​the fire, the ​thumb in ​his mouth, ​the listening birds, ‌the headless ​Reginn, and ‌Grani laden with ​the gold ‌— and ​the nearby Gök ‌stone (Sö ​327) quotes ‌the same scene ​within a ​runic serpent ‌band. The Drävle ‌runestone (U ‌1163) in ​Uppland adds a ​further Swedish ‌depiction, while ​across the North ​Sea the ‌Manx cross-slabs, ​above all the ​Kirk Andreas ‌cross, show ​Sigurðr roasting ‌Fáfnir's heart, proof ​the legend ​travelled with ​Norse settlers. In ​Norway the ‌carved portal ‌of Hylestad stave ​church (c. ‌1200) narrates ​the cycle panel ​by panel, ‌from the ‌forging of Gramr ‌to Reginn's ‌death. The ​textual tradition is ‌Icelandic and ​later: the ​heroic lays of ​the Poetic ‌Edda survive ​chiefly in the ​Codex Regius ​(GKS 2365 ‌4to, c. 1270), ​whose famous ​eight-leaf lacuna ​has cost us ‌the fullest ​form of ‌the Sigurðr lays ​— *Brot ‌af Sigurðarkviðu* ​preserves only a ‌fragment — ‌while Vǫlsunga ​saga itself (c. ​1270) survives ​in paper ​copies of the ‌lost vellum ‌NKS 1824 ​b 4to.[^1]

sections.body: The ​Sigurðr ‌cycle ‌is the ​most ​illustrated ​legend ​of ​the ‌Viking ​Age, and ​its ‌gallery ​is ‌runic. ​The ‌Ramsund ​carving (Sö ​101) ​frames ​the ​whole ‌Gnitaheiðr ​episode ‌in a ​serpent ‌band ​— ‌the ​thrust ‌from below, ​the ​roasting ‌heart, ‌the ‌burned ​thumb, ​the warning ‌birds, ​headless ​[[reginn|Reginn]] ‌— ​and ​the ‌Gök stone ​(Sö ‌327) ​and ​Drävle ​stone ​(U ‌1163) quote ‌the ​same ‌scene.[^1] ​Across ​the ‌Irish ‌Sea the ‌Manx ‌crosses, ​above ‌all ​Kirk ​Andreas and ​Jurby, ‌show ​Sigurðr ​at ​the ‌fire: ​the legend ​travelled ​with ‌the ​Norse ‌settlers.[^2] ​The ‌carved portal ​of ‌Hylestad ‌stave ​church ​(c. ​1200) ​continues the ‌cycle ‌in ​wood.

sources.citation: Ramsund, Sö 101; Gök, Sö 327; Drävle, U 1163 (the Swedish gallery).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Names ​are ‌not merely ‌labels; ​they ​are ​compressed ​worlds. **Sigurðr** ​carries ‌within ​it ​a norse ‌understanding ​of ‌victory ​under guard: ‌*sigr*, ​the ​thing ​won, ​held by ​a ‌*vǫrðr*, ​a ‌watcher — ​as ‌if ​the ‌North ​already knew ‌that ​every ​victory ‌needs defending, ‌and ‌that ​the ​guard can ‌fail. ​The ​hero ‌who ​bore the ​name ‌guarded ​the ‌hoard, the ​oath, ​and ​the ​bride, ‌and lost ‌all ​three ‌to ​a single ​draught ‌of ‌ale; ‌the name ‌outlived ​the ‌man ​by ​eight centuries ​and ‌counting. ​Unicode ​restoration returns ​that ‌world ​to ​readable ​form: the ‌eth ​that ‌softens ​the ending, ‌the ​final ‌-r ‌that marks ​him ​as ​the ​subject ‌of his ‌own ​sentence.[^1]
